Effect of the compound used as a 
nitrogen source on Collard Greens 
(Brassica oleracea) plant growth 
 
 
Plant the Moon Challenge 
Fall 2022 
Undergraduate Division 
 
Minnesota West Bluejays 
Team # 11077 
Minnesota West Community & Technical College 
Worthington, MN 
 
 
Dalton Vorwald 
Advised by Heidi Tarus, Dr. Tyler Wadzinski, and Dr. Paul Seifert 
 
 
Grant Funded by NASA’s Minnesota Space Grant Consortium

P a g e | 1 
 
Introduction 
As humans on Earth look towards future colonization of celestial bodies, we must 
address the basic needs of these colonizing humans including access to shelter, nutritious food, 
and clean water. This project focuses on addressing the human need of access to nutritious 
food that can be grown on the Moon to reduce the amount of food brought on spacecrafts. In 
order for plants to be grown for food, they need access to water and essential nutrients 
including potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen. Prior studies show that most plant essential 
nutrients are available in the composition of lunar regolith with the exception of useful nitrogen 
(Wamelink et al., 2014). Therefore, this study focuses on nitrogen and the best source of 
nitrogen that will allow plants to grow while reducing the amount of payload required on a 
spacecraft. Nitrogen is an essential macronutrient for plants and is used in the synthesis of 
proteins, nucleic acids, and some vitamins needed for growth (Clark et al., 2018). The main 
driving question for this project is to discover the trade-off between limiting the mass of 
nitrogen fertilizers brought to the moon while producing the highest yield of nutrient rich crops 
needed to feed individuals living on the moon. 
Theory 
The nitrogen sources tested were calcium nitrate tetrahydrate (Ca(NO3)2∙4H2O), 
ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3), and urea (CO(NH2)2). The three nitrogen sources have different 
molar masses and nitrogen percent compositions. They also fall into different parts of the 
nitrogen cycle, which makes comparing the trade-off between reducing the mass added to the 
space ship and the success of plant growth an important question. Calcium nitrate tetrahydrate

P a g e | 2 
 
has the lowest percent composition of nitrogen, requiring 8.4 g of compound per gram of 
nitrogen delivered. The nitrogen in calcium nitrate tetrahydrate is available immediately to 
plants in the nitrate form; however, nitrate is water soluble and thus susceptible to leaching 
which is a major cause of nitrogen loss in soil. Ammonium nitrate has a higher percent 
composition of nitrogen and requires 2.9 g of compound per gram of nitrogen delivered. 
Ammonium nitrate provides a combination of 50% nitrate which is usable to plants right away 
and 50% ammonium which must be fixed by nitrogen fixing bacteria to nitrate before it is 
usable by plants (Isleib, 2017). Therefore, ammonium nitrate is a good source of short-term and 
long-term nitrogen. Urea has the highest mass percent of nitrogen and only requires 2.1 g of 
compound per gram of nitrogen delivered, which makes it the most preferred nitrogen source 
in regard to reducing rocket payload mass. However, urea must go through a three-step 
process where it is converted to ammonia, then ammonium, and then nitrate before plants can 
use it (Mengel n.d). Similar to nitrate, urea is water soluble prior to being converted, making it 
susceptible to leaching. An additional benefit of urea is that it can be locally sourced and 
extracted from urine produced by individuals living on the moon. 
The team decided to plant Collard Greens (Brassica oleracea) because of the fast 
germination time of four to seven days, its ability to grown at lower temperatures between 4-
18 degree Celsius (40-65 degrees Fahrenheit), its ability to continuously provide highly 
nutritious leafy greens over a long period of time once mature (Palomo 2021). B. oleracea is a 
dicot plant that contains high nutrient content in the leaves. According to the U.S. Department 
of Agriculture (2019), one cup of chopped raw collard greens (36g) contains 11 calories, 1g of 
protein, 1.44g of fiber, 2g of carbohydrate, and less than 1g of fat and sugar. In addition, B.

P a g e | 3 
 
oleracea are an excellent source of many essential vitamins and minerals for humans including 
Vitamin A, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, calcium, potassium, folate, and antioxidant (Baby, n.d). The 
leaves can be eaten raw or cooked allowing for the plant to provide versatility and diversity in 
the types of food individuals can create using the plant. 
We hypothesized that ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3) would produce the largest leaves 
and most leaf surface area in the B. oleracea plants due to the ability of ammonium nitrate to 
provide both fast acting short-term nitrate and slower acting long-term nitrate that goes 
through fixation. 
Experiment & Measurement Methods 
Initial Set-Up 
The independent variable for this experiment was the type of nitrogen-containing 
compound used as a “nitrogen source”. The initial experimental set-up included four 
treatments, (1) control (no nitrogen source), (2) calcium nitrate tetrahydrate, (3) ammonium 
nitrate, and (4) urea with each treatment having 4 replicates (Figure 1). Each pot (7cm x 7cm x 
7.7cm) contained the same soil composition of 25% top soil, 25% sorghum peat moss mix, 50% 
lunar regolith by volume. Next, each nitrogen source was weighed as a pure solid and then 
mixed into the soil to achieve the recommended fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb N per 1000 ft2 
(Swift & Hammond, 2020; Kokemuller 2016; Table 1). After mixing was done, each pot was 
planted with 3-4 collard greens, Brassica oleracea, seeds and watered with 50ml of tap water. 
Over the course of the eight-week grow period, the set-up was kept indoors where the 
temperature was controlled with the set of pots placed under a grow light containing 2-18” GE 
plant and aquarium bulbs on a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark timer (Image 1). Initially the grow

P a g e | 4 
 
light was located 48 cm from the top of the pots, however, the seedlings were becoming leggy 
once germinated. After conducting some research, it was determined the light intensity was not 
high enough (Ly, 2022) and thus the light was moved down to 12cm on October 6, 2022 from 
the top of the pots to reduce leggy seedlings.

Plant Care 
Each pot was watered with 25ml of distilled water on Tuesday and Friday each week for 
the first five weeks after planting and then with 30ml of water on Tuesday and Friday during 
the last two weeks of the grow period. The increase in water during the last two weeks was 
done because the plants were showing water stress by having limp folded up leaves as the 
plants started to grow bigger. On October 11, 2022 (Day 11) a toothpick was inserted into each 
pot to mark one seedling to complete measurement on and keep during the thinning process 
which occurred on October 25, 2022 (Day 25). Thinning is a common practice in gardening and 
was done to give one seedling in each pot the best chance to grow. The height of the grow lamp 
was kept at to 12cm from the top of the pots to from October 6, 2022 to the last day of the

P a g e | 6 
 
grow period on November 18, 2022 and was kept on a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark cycle by 
using a GE 24-hour heavy duty indoor plug-in mechanical timer. The plants were kept in the 
same room through the duration of the experiment and were moved around to take 
measurements and then replaced back in generally the same location after each measuring 
event. 
Measurements 
 Germination rate was collected by visual observation of the number of germinated 
seeds in each pot each day, including weekends, for 12 days after planting. At that point, all of 
the seeds were germinated and the data collection for germination rate and time was 
complete. The soil pH was collected each Friday and the data collected did not show a 
significant change and was thus not included in this report. Once true leaves emerged the 
length of largest leaf, the number of leaves, and leaf surface area was collected on Tuesday and 
Friday of each week. The number of leaves were visually counted and recorded. The length of 
the largest leaf was measured in centimeters from the leaf base were the leaf attaches to the 
petiole to the tip of the leaf. Leaf surface area was collected using the LeafByte App, 
https://zoegp.science/leafbyte. This was done by holding up a scale (a white piece of paper 
with four black dots in the shape of a square) behind the leaf, taking a picture with a smart 
phone, identifying the scale, and having the app calculate the square centimeters of the leaf 
(Image Set 2).

In addition, a picture of the entire set-up was taken at least once a week (See Appendix 
B: Photos). Records of the data collected was kept on paper next to the set up and was entered 
each week into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet each week for data analysis. 
Analysis & Results 
Data was stored, analyzed with linear fit models to calculate rates, and graphed using 
Microsoft Excel. ANOVA statistical tests were done using a free online website, Statistics 
Kingdom - https://www.statskingdom.com/.

Soil pH & Germination Rate 
The soil pH of each pot did not change over the course of the eight weeks and stayed 
around a neutral pH of 6-7. Because the pH did not change over time the raw data and results 
are not included in this report. The germination data shows that the seeds in the control, 
calcium nitrate tetrahydrate, and ammonium nitrate pots germinated about 1 day before the 
seeds planted in the urea supplemented pots (Appendix A Table 2). 
Number of Leaves 
The raw data for the number of leaves is available in Appendix A Table 3. A linear fit 
calculated the average rate of leaf production during the measurement period was 0.06 
leaves/day for the control plants, 0.12 leaves/day for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate plants, 
0.10 leaves/day for the ammonium nitrate plants, and 0.12/day for the urea plants (Figure 2 
and Appendix A Table 3).

P a g e | 9 
 
Figure 2. Effect of compound used as a nitrogen source on the number of leaves. Each 
treatment contained four plants where the number of leaves was measured and averaged. 
 
 
 
A one-way ANOVA was performed to compared the effect of the compound used as a 
nitrogen source on the rate of leaf production. The test revealed that there is a statistically 
significant difference in the leaf growth rate between at least two groups (F(3,12)= [9.1469], p = 
0.002). Tukey’s HSD Test for multiple comparisons found that the mean value of leaf growth 
rate was significantly different between the control and the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group 
(p = 0.00372, 95% C.I. = [0.019, 0.09448]), the control and the ammonium nitrate group (p = 
0.03663, 95% C.I. = [0.00228, 0.07775]), and the control and the urea group (p = 0.002946, 95% 
C.I. = [0.02076, 0.09623]). There was no statistically significant difference in the leaf growth rate 
between the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate and ammonium nitrate group (p=0.5709), the calcium 
nitrate tetrahydrate and urea group (p=0.999) or between the ammonium nitrate and urea 
group (p=0.4926).

Length of Largest Leaf 
The raw data for length of the largest leaf is available in Appendix A Table 4. A linear fit 
calculated the average rate of leaf length growth during the measurement period was 0.04 
cm/day for the control plants, 0.07 cm/day for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate plants, 0.08 
cm/day for the ammonium nitrate plants, and 0.10 cm/day for the urea plants.

Leaf Surface Area 
The raw data for leaf surface area is available in Appendix A Table 5. A linear fit 
calculated the average growth rate of the leaf surface area during the measurement period was 
0.23 cm2/day for the control plants, 1.67 cm2/day for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate plants, 
1.7 cm2/day for the ammonium nitrate plants, and 1.94 cm2/day for the urea plants (Figure 4).

Discussion & Conclusion 
 
The overall results show that B. oleracea grew significantly more in terms of leaf length, 
number of leaves, and leaf surface area in the presence of a compound used as a nitrogen 
source compared to when no nitrogen source was provided. Based on the data collected the

P a g e | 15 
 
Minnesota West Bluejays team recommends adding one of the three tested nitrogen 
compounds using a fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb N per 1000 ft2 to a 25% top soil, 25% 
sorghum peat moss mix, 50% lunar regolith (by volume) soil mixture when growing B. oleracea. 
These results partially support the team’s hypothesis because the plants provided with a 
nitrogen source grew better compared to the control plants; however, the team also 
hypothesized that ammonium nitrate would show the best growth. 
The data did not support the second part of the hypothesis since there was no major 
significant difference in plant growth between the three different nitrogen sources. The overall 
goal of the project was to find the nitrogen source that produced plant growth while reducing 
the payload on the spacecraft; therefore, the team recommends the use of urea as a nitrogen 
source when growing B. oleracea. Urea only requires 2.1 g of compound per gram of nitrogen 
delivered making it the most weight efficient nitrogen source tested in this experiment. In 
addition, the requirement to bring urea from Earth of the Moon may not be needed as urea can 
potentially be extracted from the urine of humans living on the Moon. Human typically produce 
12 to 20 g of urea in urine over the course of 24-hours (Jacob, 2021). Depending on the number 
of humans and the nitrogen requirements of the plants being grown, this amount of urea could 
be sufficient to avoid brining urea to the Moon. Investigations into the method and efficiency of 
urea extraction from human urine would be needed. 
 
Although not specifically analyzed, the B. oleracea plants provided with urea took 
approximately one day longer to germinate (Appendix A Table 2) and appeared to have slower 
growth for leaf length and surface area at the beginning; however, the urea plants quickly 
caught up with the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate and the ammonium nitrate plants and started

P a g e | 16 
 
to show more growth at the end of the experiment (Figure 3 and Figure 4). The slower start to 
the urea plants could be accounted for the fact that urea must go through a three-step process 
where it is converted to ammonia, then ammonium, and then nitrate before plants can use it 
(Mengel n.d). It would be interesting to have the experiment run longer to see if the high 
growth rate trend for the urea supplemented B. oleracea plants would continue and become 
significant. 
Future experiments could involve comparing the nutritional content of the B. oleracea 
plants for each of the treatments would allow the team to give a more informed 
recommendation as there could potentially be a tradeoff between payload the nutritional value 
of the plants. The compounds used as a nitrogen source were added during the initial set-up, so 
it would be interesting to look how reapplication of fertilizer would influence B. oleracea plant 
growth. In addition, replicating the set-up used during this experiment using other plant species 
is recommended to see if urea is a good nitrogen sources for other nutrient rich plants that 
could be used as a food source for human on the Moon.
